stops.name: Newington Butts, the smith's third child
stops.date_confidence: attested to 22 September 1791 by the Royal Institution's biographical record. No street address survives; the coordinates mark the historical parish of Newington Butts, now Southwark, not a house. The father's northern origin is standard biographical tradition and is not carried by any source fetched for this file
stops.campa: James Faraday, a journeyman smith come south for work, is living in Newington Butts, a parish of market gardens and tanneries below the river, when his third child is born on the twenty second of September. The father's health is poor and the trade is precarious. What the record keeps is the parish and the date; the house is gone and was never written down. The boy will be given no more schooling than reading, writing and the beginnings of arithmetic at a common day school, and no grammar school and no university will ever have him on its books.
suggested_refs: The parish of Newington Butts, Surrey, absorbed into Southwark

stops.name: Jacob's Well Mews, the loaf divided by fourteen
stops.date_confidence: [R] The move to Marylebone is dated 1796 in the chronology and c.1791-1804 in the geography of the research pool, a contradiction left standing here. The Jacob's Well Mews address is early biographical tradition and appears in none of the institutional sources fetched for this file. The fourteen portions of bread are testimony, not an audited record. Coordinates corrected to the mews itself rather than the Manchester Square side
stops.campa: The family moves north of the river to rooms over a coach house in a mews behind Manchester Square, a smith's household kept respectable on very little. Marylebone will be his neighbourhood for the next thirty years. The tradition that comes down from his own account has him given a loaf to last a week, which he divides into fourteen portions, one for each morning and each evening. It is early testimony rather than an audited record, and every life of him written since has repeated it.
suggested_refs: Jacob's Well Mews, W1U, and the poor rate books of St Marylebone
sources: early biographical tradition, unconfirmed against a primary source in this research pool

stops.name: Blandford Street, the bindery of George Riebau
stops.date_confidence: attested to 7 October 1805 for the formal indenture, and to 1804 for the errand-boy year, by the Royal Institution record. The street NUMBER is contradicted inside the research pool: the chronology gives 2 Blandford Street, the geography and English Heritage's blue plaque page give 48. The contradiction is not resolved here; the pin is Blandford Street, within about fifty metres either way
stops.campa: At about thirteen he is taken on as errand boy by George Riebau, bookseller and bookbinder, carrying newspapers out on loan in the morning and collecting them again at night. On the seventh of October 1805 he is bound apprentice for seven years, and Riebau lets him read what passes over the bench. He reads the article on electricity in an encyclopaedia awaiting rebinding, and Jane Marcet's Conversations on Chemistry. He begins repeating what they describe with bottles and a homemade electrical machine, between jobs, in the shop.
suggested_refs: English Heritage blue plaque, 48 Blandford Street, Marylebone, erected 1876: MICHAEL FARADAY MAN OF SCIENCE. APPRENTICE HERE. B.1791. D.1867.

stops.name: Dorset Street, the City Philosophical Society
stops.date_confidence: [R] The membership of John Tatum's society is in the Royal Institution record but is tagged as tradition in the research pool, and no verified street address was reached; the coordinates are an approximate central London placeholder and should not be read as an attested site. The first surviving Faraday letter to Benjamin Abbott is dated 12 and 13 July 1812 in the Epsilon correspondence edition, correcting the 1811 given elsewhere in the pool
stops.campa: On Wednesday evenings he pays a shilling to hear John Tatum lecture on natural philosophy in a room hired for the purpose, among clerks and shopmen who have taught themselves whatever they know. He learns here to stand up and speak, and criticises his own delivery afterwards in writing. From July 1812 he begins writing to Benjamin Abbott, a young Quaker clerk, and argues out rhetoric, chemistry and self improvement with him at enormous length. Where the society actually met is not now recorded.
suggested_refs: Epsilon: The Michael Faraday Collection, letters Faraday0003 onward, the Abbott correspondence

stops.name: Royal Institution, the last four lectures of Humphry Davy
stops.date_confidence: attested by the Royal Institution record: tickets from William Dance, Davy's final four lectures in 1812, the bound manuscript of roughly three hundred pages sent to Davy the same year. The month of the lecture course is not pinned in the pool and February is used to order the segment. The pin is the Royal Institution coordinate already carried in charles_babbage.journey.json and nikola_tesla.journey.json
stops.campa: William Dance, a member of the Institution and a customer at the bindery, gives the apprentice tickets to Humphry Davy's final four lectures. Faraday sits in the gallery of the theatre in Albemarle Street and takes down everything said. At home he works the notes up with drawings of the apparatus, indexes them, and binds them himself into some three hundred pages. He sends the volume to Davy with a letter asking for any employment whatever in science. Davy answers courteously and has no post to give. The indenture runs out and he goes back to bookbinding.
suggested_refs: Faraday's bound manuscript of Davy's 1812 lectures, Royal Institution collection
sources: charles_babbage.journey.json, stop 'Albemarle Street, lecturing at the Royal Institution' (shared pin)

stops.name: Royal Institution, the post that opens by a fight
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 March 1813 by the Royal Institution record, including the detail that the vacancy arose from an assistant dismissed for fighting. The wage, the rooms and the allowance of candles and fuel are standard biography and are not itemised in the sources fetched for this file
stops.campa: A laboratory assistant is dismissed for fighting in the building, and Davy sends for the bookbinder. On the first of March he is appointed Chemical Assistant at the Royal Institution, with rooms at the top of the house. From this address he will work for fifty two years, and he will leave it only when he is too infirm to keep going up and down to the basement laboratory where nearly everything he does gets done. He is twenty one years old, and a few months out of his apprenticeship.
suggested_refs: The basement laboratory at 21 Albemarle Street, preserved as the Faraday Museum

stops.name: Royal Institution, rules for a lecturer
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the wording, quoted verbatim by John Tyndall in the Dictionary of National Biography, vol. 18 (1889). The date is Tyndall's c.1813 and the month is set to order the segment. Tyndall places these letters AFTER Faraday was already in the laboratory with Davy, which corrects the framing in the research pool that put them before he held any post
stops.campa: He is in the laboratory daily now, and he is thinking about the theatre downstairs as hard as he is thinking about the bench. To Abbott he sets out point by point what a lecture ought to be: the size of the room, the ventilation, the pace of delivery, the vice of a fixed manner, the discourtesy of reading aloud from paper. He is twenty two years old and has been an assistant since March. He has not yet given a public lecture in his life. He keeps to these rules for the next forty years.
stops.quote: A lecturer should appear easy and collected, undaunted and unconcerned. His thoughts about him, and his mind clear and free for the contemplation and description of his subject. His whole behaviour should evince respect for his audience, and he should in no case forget that he is in their presence.
stops.quote_source: Michael Faraday to Benjamin Abbott, c.1813, quoted in John Tyndall, 'Faraday, Michael', Dictionary of National Biography, vol. 18 (1889)
suggested_refs: The Abbott letters on lecturing, Epsilon: The Michael Faraday Collection
sources: John Tyndall, DNB vol. 18 (1889), Wikisource digitised text

stops.name: Plymouth, the cartel to Morlaix
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Dictionary of National Biography gives departure from London on 13 October 1813, and the sailing by cartel from Plymouth to Morlaix under a Napoleonic passport is from the account of Davy's tour. This CORRECTS the research pool's chronology, which gave the departure place as Dover. The tour runs to April 1815
stops.campa: Davy holds a passport from Napoleon to travel in an enemy country and takes with him his wife Jane, her maid, and Faraday as scientific assistant and secretary. The valet engaged for the journey refuses at the last moment to leave England. Faraday takes on his duties as well, so that he crosses to Europe as an assistant philosopher and a manservant in the same person. The party leaves London on the thirteenth of October and sails by cartel from Plymouth into Morlaix in Brittany. He has never before been more than a few miles outside London.
suggested_refs: Bowers and Symons (eds.), 'Curiosity Perfectly Satisfyed': Faraday's Travels in Europe 1813-1815 (1991)

stops.name: Paris, the Institut de France
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the meetings with Ampere and Gay-Lussac at Paris, per the account of Davy's tour; the month is inferred, since the party left London on 13 October and sailed by way of Morlaix, so Paris falls later in October or November. The research pool also placed Alexander von Humboldt with the party, at Geneva; no source reached here puts Humboldt at Geneva, and no source reached here confirms a Faraday meeting with him at Paris either. The claim is flagged, not carried
stops.campa: In an enemy capital under police surveillance the party is received by the French chemists. Faraday is presented to Ampere, and hears Gay-Lussac on the new substance drawn out of the ash of burnt seaweed, the one Davy will shortly satisfy himself is an element in its own right. He is nine months out of the bindery and has never been in such a room before. In the lodgings afterwards he writes up the travel journal, settles the accounts and cleans the apparatus.
suggested_refs: humboldt.journey.json, Paris stops of 1804-1827: whether Faraday met Humboldt on this tour is an open question in the sources reached here
sources: Bowers and Symons (eds.), 'Curiosity Perfectly Satisfyed' (1991), as summarised by the Royal Institution

stops.name: Florence, the burning lens of the Grand Duke
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the experiment: the diamond combustion using the Grand Duke of Tuscany's burning glass, with Faraday assisting, is confirmed in the account of Davy's tour. This CORRECTS the research pool's label, which attributed the instrument to the Accademia del Cimento, defunct since 1667. The month is inferred to order the southward leg; the pool gives only 1814
stops.campa: Southward through Montpellier, then along the coast road by Nice and Genoa, and over into Tuscany. In Florence the grand ducal collection yields a great burning lens, and Davy sets it to bring the sun to a point on a diamond held in a vessel of oxygen. Faraday works the apparatus and writes down the result. The diamond burns away. What comes off it is carbon dioxide and nothing else, and the hardest substance known is shown to be the same element as soot. A sample of Tuscan caustic lime goes into the baggage to be carried home.
suggested_refs: The grand ducal burning lens, Museo Galileo, Florence

stops.name: Milan, the man who made the current
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1814 in the account of Davy's tour, which places the meeting with Alessandro Volta at Milan and the party continuing north to Geneva from there. This CORRECTS the research pool in two places: it dated Milan to 1815 and put the Volta meeting at Geneva. The Rome and Naples legs named in the campa rest on the pool's account of the Bowers and Symons edition of the travel journals, which was not fetched directly, and are [R]
stops.campa: After a spring in Rome and a stretch at Naples the party turns north, and in June it is at Milan, where they are received by Alessandro Volta. His pile of zinc and silver discs made the first steady current, and so made possible everything Faraday will spend the next fifty years doing. The meeting is a courtesy between one famous chemist and another, and Faraday is there as the assistant who carries the chest. Volta is sixty nine and has fourteen years to live. Faraday enters the visit in the travel journal and says little more about it.
suggested_refs: Volta's pile and the voltaic apparatus, Tempio Voltiano, Como

stops.name: Geneva, the letter about the clouds
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the quotation, from the Geneva letter to Abbott of 1814 quoted by Tyndall in the DNB. [A] for the de la Rive friendship, which is the one element of the pool's Geneva stop that survives verification; the pool also placed Volta, Humboldt and Augustin de Candolle here, and all three are removed, Volta to Milan and the other two for want of any source. The month orders the segment
stops.campa: At Geneva the party is with the physicist Auguste de la Rive, who treats the assistant as a colleague rather than as baggage, and who will be a friend of Faraday's for the rest of his life. From here Faraday writes to Abbott about the year behind him and about the difficulties in it, which he describes as clouds that came between him and prosperity and which turned out, in the event, to have refreshed him. He is candid that the journey has cost him something. He has been on the road nine months, and there are nine more to come.
stops.quote: clouds, which intervened between me and the sun of prosperity, but which I found were refreshing, reserving to me that tone and vigour of mind which prosperity alone would enervate and ultimately destroy.
stops.quote_source: Michael Faraday to Benjamin Abbott, Geneva, 1814, quoted in John Tyndall, 'Faraday, Michael', Dictionary of National Biography, vol. 18 (1889)
suggested_refs: The correspondence of Faraday and Auguste de la Rive, Epsilon: The Michael Faraday Collection
sources: John Tyndall, DNB vol. 18 (1889), Wikisource digitised text

stops.name: Royal Institution, the caustic lime of Tuscany
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1816 by the bibliographic listing of 'Analysis of Native Caustic Lime of Tuscany' and the Royal Institution record; the month is unknown and defaults to January. The work with William Thomas Brande and the alloy experiments with James Stodart are dated 1815-1820 in the research pool's geography lens
stops.campa: Back in Albemarle Street from April 1815 at a raised salary, he works under William Thomas Brande as assistant and, more and more, as an analyst on his own account. In 1816 the Quarterly Journal of Science prints his analysis of a native caustic lime from Tuscany, a sample he carried home in his own baggage. It is a short and exact piece of chemistry, of no importance to anybody, and it is the first thing he ever publishes. Some four hundred and fifty papers follow it. In the same years he and the cutler James Stodart work on alloy steels.
suggested_refs: 'Analysis of Native Caustic Lime of Tuscany', Quarterly Journal of Science (1816)
sources: bibliographic listing per the research pool

stops.name: Paul's Alley, the Barbican, the marriage and the confession
stops.date_confidence: attested to 12 June 1821 for the marriage. Two corrections to the research pool: the confession of faith came a MONTH after the wedding, in mid July, not on the same day; and under the Marriage Act 1753, in force until 1836, a Sandemanian meeting house could not solemnise a valid marriage, so the wedding venue as given in the pool is doubtful and is not asserted here. The pin is Paul's Alley, where the congregation had met since 1778, within about 150 metres of where the alley ran off Redcross Street
stops.campa: Sarah Barnard is the daughter of Edward Barnard, a London silversmith and an elder of the Sandemanian church that meets in Paul's Alley off Redcross Street in the Barbican. They marry on the twelfth of June 1821. A month later, having said nothing to her about it beforehand, he makes his own confession of faith before the congregation and is received into the communion. It is a body of perhaps a hundred souls in London, with no paid ministry and no doctrine beyond the plain text. He stays in it for the remaining forty six years of his life.
stops.quote: Amongst these records and events, I here insert the date of one which, as a source of honour and happiness, far exceeds all the rest. We were married on June 12, 1821.
stops.quote_source: Michael Faraday, entry of 25 January 1847 in his diploma book, recording the 1821 marriage; transcribed by John Tyndall in Faraday as a Discoverer
suggested_refs: The Sandemanian meeting house, Paul's Alley, Redcross Street, occupied by the congregation from autumn 1778
sources: John Tyndall, Faraday as a Discoverer, archive.org item faradayasdiscove00tynduoft

stops.name: Royal Institution, the wire that turns and does not stop
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1821 by the Royal Institution record for the demonstration of continuous electromagnetic rotation and for the priority dispute that followed; the month is traditionally September and is used here to order the segment. His appointment as Assistant Superintendent of the House falls in the same year: the pool's title, Superintendent of the House and Laboratory, is a later one and is corrected here against the Royal Institution's own page
stops.campa: A year after Oersted found that a current deflects a compass needle, Faraday is asked for a review of the whole state of electromagnetism, and repeats everything in the basement to see it for himself. Nobody has produced continuous motion. He stands a magnet upright in a bath of mercury and hangs a wire so that it swings free; when the current runs, the wire circles the magnet steadily and goes on circling. It is the first electric motor. Wollaston had predicted rotation and failed to obtain it, and the charge that Faraday took the idea without acknowledgement will follow him for years.
suggested_refs: Faraday's electromagnetic rotation apparatus, 1821, Royal Institution collection
sources: Royal Society publication record per the research pool

stops.name: Somerset House, one black ball
stops.date_confidence: [R] The date of election, 8 January 1824, and the single adverse ballot are in the Royal Institution record; the attribution of that ballot to Davy is traditional and not provable. The venue, Somerset House as the Royal Society's premises until 1857, is general historical record and was not re-fetched. Charles Babbage's support for the candidacy and the long friendship are DOSSIER-ONLY in the research pool, tagged [R] there, and are carried here with that tag
stops.campa: Davy, his patron, opposes the election and asks him to withdraw it; Faraday declines, and answers that Davy is free to strike the name off himself. The year before, he had liquefied chlorine by heating its hydrate in a sealed tube, work in which Davy also claimed a share. Charles Babbage, born three months after him and moving in the same reforming scientific London, is among those said to have supported the candidacy. On the eighth of January 1824 he is elected Fellow of the Royal Society, with a single black ball in the box against him.
suggested_refs: charles_babbage.journey.json, on the shared reforming circle of London science in the 1820s
'On the Condensation of Several Gases into Liquids' (1823)
sources: K. K. Schwarz, 'Faraday and Babbage', per the research dossier, unverified here

stops.name: Royal Institution, bicarburet of hydrogen
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1825 by the Royal Institution record and the paper 'On New Compounds of Carbon and Hydrogen'; the month is unknown and June is used to order the segment. The Directorship of the Laboratory and the founding of the Friday Evening Discourses and the Christmas Lectures are dated 1825 in the same record
stops.campa: A gas company sends him the oily residue left standing in its cylinders, condensed out of illuminating gas made from whale oil. He distils it, freezes it, distils it again, and separates a clear liquid that boils low and burns with a smoky flame. He calls it bicarburet of hydrogen. It is benzene, and the entire chemistry of the aromatic ring begins in a barrel of waste. In the same year he becomes Director of the Laboratory and starts the Friday Evening Discourses, and with them the Christmas Lectures for young people.
suggested_refs: 'On New Compounds of Carbon and Hydrogen' (1825); Faraday's sample of benzene, Royal Institution collection

stops.name: Woolwich, chemistry for the cadets
stops.date_confidence: CORRECTED against the Royal Institution's own page, which gives 1830-1851 for the professorship of chemistry at the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich, and lists 1829 separately as the year he was appointed Scientific Adviser to the Admiralty. The research pool's 1829-1852 conflated the two appointments. Month unknown, defaults to January
stops.campa: From 1830 he goes downriver to the Royal Military Academy at Woolwich to lecture chemistry to cadets, and keeps it up for twenty one years. The Royal Institution has never paid him enough. The Woolwich chair, the Admiralty advice he began giving the year before, and the analytical work he takes in privately are what keep the household. Later in the decade he begins turning down the private consulting, which is the profitable part of it, in order to have his days for the laboratory, and his income falls by more than half.
suggested_refs: The Royal Military Academy, Woolwich Common, and its chemistry course 1830-1851

stops.name: Royal Institution, the ring of soft iron
stops.date_confidence: attested to 29 August 1831 by the Royal Institution's own object record for the induction ring. The quotation is Faraday's, dated 1831 by Tyndall in the DNB
stops.campa: He takes a ring of soft iron, winds insulated copper wire round one half of it and more wire round the other, connects the second coil to a galvanometer and the first to a battery. Closing the circuit swings the needle. Holding it closed does nothing at all. Opening it swings the needle back the other way. Nothing crosses the iron but change. It is the twenty ninth of August, and he spends the following months finding out how much of the effect he can get out of it.
stops.quote: I have rather been desirous of discovering new facts and new relations dependent on magneto-electric induction, than of exalting the force of those already obtained, being assured that the latter would find their full development hereafter.
stops.quote_source: Michael Faraday, 1831, quoted in John Tyndall, 'Faraday, Michael', Dictionary of National Biography, vol. 18 (1889)
suggested_refs: Faraday's induction ring of 1831, Royal Institution iconic objects collection
sources: Royal Institution, 'Iconic Objects' collection page, rigb.org

stops.name: Royal Institution, the copper disc between the poles
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1831, a few months after the induction ring, by the Royal Institution object record; the day is the one conventionally given and is used to order the segment. The date of the first Experimental Researches paper reaching the Royal Society, November 1831, is tagged [R] in the research pool: the Philosophical Transactions page returned HTTP 403 and could not be confirmed
stops.campa: In the autumn he sets a copper disc turning between the poles of a great horseshoe magnet, with one contact at the axle and one on the rim, and draws off a current that does not stop while the disc goes round. It is the first machine to make electricity out of motion alone, with no battery and no chemistry in it anywhere. The paper goes to the Royal Society in November as the first of the Experimental Researches in Electricity, a series he will carry to thirty parts across twenty four years, numbering the paragraphs straight through from the first to the last.
suggested_refs: Faraday's disc generator of 1831, Royal Institution iconic objects collection
Experimental Researches in Electricity, series 1-30, Philosophical Transactions
sources: Royal Institution, 'Iconic Objects' collection page, rigb.org

stops.name: Paul's Alley, ordained deacon
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1 July 1832, which UPGRADES the research pool's [R] tag; the same source gives the two eldership terms, 1840-1844 and 1860-1864, the exclusion from the communion in 1844, and the resignation of the eldership on 5 June 1864. The circumstances of the 1844 exclusion are not established in anything reached here
stops.campa: On the first of July he is ordained deacon of the Sandemanian church, which keeps no paid ministry and no clergy in the ordinary sense; a deacon reads, exhorts, and looks after the poor of the congregation out of its collections. He is ten months past the induction ring and the whole of the Experimental Researches lies ahead of him, and he takes on the visiting of the sick in a body of about a hundred people. He will be an elder twice, from 1840 to 1844 and again from 1860 to 1864. In 1844 he is excluded from the communion for a time, in circumstances the surviving record does not explain. He resigns the eldership on the fifth of June 1864.
suggested_refs: Geoffrey Cantor, Michael Faraday: Sandemanian and Scientist (1991)

stops.name: Royal Institution, the words made with Whewell
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1833 by the Royal Institution record for the laws of electrolysis, the Whewell correspondence over terminology, and the appointment as first Fullerian Professor of Chemistry. Month unknown, defaults to January
stops.campa: Working out the quantitative laws by which a current decomposes a solution, he needs vocabulary that smuggles no theory in with it, and writes to William Whewell at Cambridge for help. Between them they settle on electrode, electrolyte, anode, cathode, ion, anion and cation, built out of Greek so as to say going and coming and nothing further. The words are still in use, unaltered. The same year the Institution makes him first Fullerian Professor of Chemistry, on John Fuller's endowment, a chair held for life with no obligation to lecture at all.
suggested_refs: The Faraday-Whewell correspondence on electrochemical nomenclature, 1833-1834, Epsilon

stops.name: Royal Institution, the word humbug
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION carried, not resolved: the DNB puts the Melbourne interview and the pension arrangement at c.1835, with Melbourne using the word humbug and apologising later in writing; the Royal Institution's page dates the award of the Civil List pension to 1836. Both readings are given here, the interview at 1835 and the award at 1836. The interview's venue is not recorded in the pool, so the stop sits at Faraday's own pin rather than staging him anywhere he may not have been. Month set to order the segment
stops.campa: A Civil List pension of three hundred pounds a year is proposed for him. He is sent to see Lord Melbourne, the Prime Minister, who says in his hearing that such pensions are a piece of humbug. Faraday takes his hat, tells him he can accept nothing on those terms, and goes home. He is forty four, he is the most celebrated experimental philosopher in England, and he is living on an institutional salary in rooms at the top of a house he does not own. Friends intervene, Melbourne writes an apology, and the pension is awarded.
suggested_refs: Lord Melbourne's written apology to Faraday, c.1835

stops.name: Royal Institution, the room lined with metal
stops.date_confidence: [R] The demonstration of electrostatic shielding in a metal-lined room is dated 1836 in the Royal Institution record and is tagged [R] in the research pool. The dimensions of the cube and the detail of the gauze covering are standard in the biographical literature and are not carried by any source fetched for this file. Month set to order the segment
stops.campa: He builds a cube in the lecture theatre, frames it in wood, covers it over with wire gauze and paper, and has it charged from a machine until sparks come off the outside of it. Then he climbs in with his most sensitive electrometers and shuts himself up inside. Nothing. The charge stays entirely on the outer surface, and no instrument he has can find the least influence within. Electrical force is a matter of the surface, and of the space around a body, and not of the substance of it.
suggested_refs: Faraday's ice pail experiment and the shielding cube of 1836, Royal Institution collection

stops.name: Trinity House, Tower Hill, adviser to the lights
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1836 by the Royal Institution record, with the role running to 1865; the Admiralty adviser's post is dated 1829 in the same source. Month set to order the segment after the shielding experiment
stops.campa: The Corporation of Trinity House, which keeps the lights and buoys of England and Wales, appoints him its scientific adviser. For twenty nine years he comes down to Tower Hill, and goes out to the lights themselves, on the ventilation of lantern rooms, the smoke of oil lamps, the corrosion of reflectors, lightning conductors on towers, and the endless proposals of inventors who want the Corporation's money. It is unglamorous and it never stops, and he treats it exactly as he treats the laboratory. He is adviser to the Admiralty as well, from 1829.
suggested_refs: Trinity House lighthouse papers, Faraday's reports 1836-1865

stops.name: Royal Institution, the scraps of pencilled paper
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION carried: the research pool dates the breakdown to 1839, the DNB dates it to 1841 and says it lasted about three years. Read together, 1839 is defensible as the onset of the memory trouble and 1841 as the collapse; the stop is dated 1841 and the earlier onset is stated in the campa. NO medical cause is established: see A. J. Larner, 'Michael Faraday's loss of memory revisited', Journal of Medical Biography (2021), whose abstract was reviewed via the pool and not fetched directly. The quotation is verbatim from Tyndall, who describes seeing the original scraps
stops.campa: From about 1839 he cannot hold a train of thought, cannot recall what he did the day before, and cannot bear conversation. By 1841 the laboratory work has stopped almost entirely, and it stays stopped for about three years. He writes notes to visitors in pencil on scraps of paper rather than speak to them. He is forty nine. No cause has ever been established: poisoning by the mercury he has worked over for twenty years, and plain exhaustion, have both been argued, and neither proved.
stops.quote: when I say I am not able to bear much talking, it means really, and without any mistake, or equivocation, or oblique meaning, or implication, or subterfuge, or omission, that I am not able; being at present rather weak in the head, and able to work no more.
stops.quote_source: Michael Faraday, pencilled note of the breakdown period, quoted in John Tyndall, 'Faraday, Michael', Dictionary of National Biography, vol. 18 (1889)
suggested_refs: A. J. Larner, 'Michael Faraday's loss of memory revisited', Journal of Medical Biography (2021)
sources: John Tyndall, DNB vol. 18 (1889), Wikisource digitised text
Dictionary of National Biography, vol. 18 (1889), on the 1841 breakdown

stops.name: Interlaken, the cloutnail shop
stops.date_confidence: attested: the journal entry is dated Interlaken, 2 August 1841, and quoted verbatim by Tyndall in the DNB. The Switzerland journey with Sarah and her brother George Barnard is confirmed by the DNB, which UPGRADES the research pool's [R] tag; the pool's Geneva coordinates for this trip are dropped, since no source places him there in 1841, and the pin is Interlaken, where the journal entry was written
stops.campa: Ordered to rest, he goes to Switzerland with Sarah and with her brother George Barnard, a painter, and spends the summer walking. He keeps a journal and puts no science into it. At Interlaken he stops to watch men making cloutnails, the short flat headed nails used on boot soles, hammered out one at a time over a small forge. He is fifty years old and the son of a blacksmith. He stands in the doorway of the shop until the work is done, and afterwards writes it into the journal.
stops.quote: Cloutnail-making goes on here rather considerably, and is a very neat and pretty operation to observe. I love a smith's shop and anything relating to smithery. My father was a smith.

stops.name: Haswell, County Durham, ninety five dead
stops.date_confidence: attested to 28 September 1844 for the explosion, which killed 95 miners; the Home Office inquiry by Faraday and Charles Lyell reported in 1845 or 1846, and the research pool notes that Wikipedia dates the report to 1846 while the explosion is 1844. Both can be true and neither is resolved here
stops.campa: An explosion at the Haswell pit in County Durham kills ninety five men and boys. The Home Office sends Faraday and the geologist Charles Lyell north to find out why. They go down the shaft themselves, question the survivors and the viewers, and report that firedamp was fired at a naked light and that the ventilation was inadequate. They press further, that fine coal dust hanging in the air carried the blast and made it worse. The report is addressed to a government which at that date has no inspectorate and no power to compel a colliery to do anything at all.

stops.name: Royal Institution, the magnet that turns a ray
stops.date_confidence: attested to 13 September 1845 by the Royal Institution record. The heavy glass is the material left over from the optical glass project the Royal Society had set him in the 1820s and which he abandoned
stops.campa: He has been trying for years to catch some action of magnetism upon light, and has failed with air, with water, with ordinary glass. On the thirteenth of September he takes a block of the heavy lead borate glass left over from the optical glass work he gave up twenty years earlier, and sends polarised light through it lengthwise between the poles of an electromagnet. The plane of polarisation turns. Nothing in the glass has altered. What has altered is the space the light is crossing.
suggested_refs: Faraday's heavy glass block and the magneto-optical apparatus of 1845, Royal Institution collection

stops.name: Royal Institution, the substances that flee a magnet
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1845 by the Royal Institution record for the demonstration of diamagnetism; the month is set to order the segment after the 13 September result. The list of substances he suspended between the poles is standard in the biographical literature and is [R] here, being carried by no source fetched for this file
stops.campa: Working with the same heavy glass and the same electromagnet, he finds that a bar of it hung between the poles will not point along the field as iron does, but sets itself square across it. Nearly every substance he tries answers a magnet, and most of them answer by being pushed weakly away from it. He calls the property diamagnetism. Magnetism stops being an oddity belonging to iron. He goes on hanging things up between the poles, metals and wood and water and flesh, whatever the laboratory has in it.
suggested_refs: Experimental Researches in Electricity, series 20-21, on diamagnetism

He is fifty six, with a pension and a professorship held for life, and has lived until now in two rooms at the top of an institution belonging to somebody else. He accepts, and then finds the place needs a great deal of work. He tells the Crown he cannot pay for it himself. stops.name: Royal Institution, the chemical history of a candle
stops.date_confidence: attested: the six lectures on the chemical history of a candle were delivered as the Christmas Lectures for young people and published in 1861 in William Crookes's edition. The research pool dates delivery to 1848 and publication to 1861; the exact opening date of the 1848 course is not in the pool and 27 December is used to order the segment. The quotation is verbatim from the Project Gutenberg text of the 1861 edition, Lecture I
stops.campa: For the Christmas Lectures he takes one candle and, over six evenings in front of an audience of children, gets the whole of chemistry out of it: combustion, the products of combustion, the composition of air, the composition of water, respiration, the carbon in a breath. He lights it, blows it out, relights the smoke at a distance from the wick, puts a glass tube into the dark centre of the flame and draws off unburnt wax as a vapour. William Crookes takes the course down and publishes it in 1861, and it has not been out of print since.
stops.quote: There is not a law under which any part of this universe is governed which does not come into play, and is touched upon in these phenomena. There is no better, there is no more open door by which you can enter into the study of natural philosophy, than by considering the physical phenomena of a candle.
stops.quote_source: Michael Faraday, A Course of Six Lectures on the Chemical History of a Candle, ed. William Crookes (1861), Lecture I; Project Gutenberg e-text 14474

stops.name: Royal Institution, the laboratory book of the nineteenth of March
stops.date_confidence: attested to 19 March 1849, traced to the printed primary source: Henry Bence Jones, The Life and Letters of Faraday (1870), vol. II, p. 248, which introduces it as written in the laboratory book on that day, equating to Diary entry 10,040. This UPGRADES the research pool's [R] tag on the famous one-liner and CORRECTS its context: the entry concerns his speculations on gravity and electricity, not the gold and diamond work. The circulating quotation is only the first half of the sentence; the full sentence is given here
stops.campa: He is fifty seven and has been trying, on and off for years, to find some relation between gravity and electricity, dropping helices of wire and hanging weights and finding nothing at all. On the nineteenth of March he fills page after page of the laboratory book with what such a relation would have to look like and what experiments would put it to the test. He finds nothing this time either. Then he writes, in capitals, that all of it is a dream, and goes straight on to the next line.
stops.quote: ALL THIS IS A DREAM. Still examine it by a few experiments. Nothing is too wonderful to be true, if it be consistent with the laws of nature; and in such things as these, experiment is the best test of such consistency.
stops.quote_source: Michael Faraday, laboratory book, 19 March 1849, printed in Henry Bence Jones, The Life and Letters of Faraday (1870), vol. II, p. 248

stops.name: Royal Institution, the answer to Lady Lovelace

He answers that he belongs to a very small and despised sect of Christians, known if known at all as Sandemanians, and that their hope is founded on the faith as it is in Christ. He does not argue for it. In fifty years he never carries it into a lecture or a paper. What she made of the answer is not recorded.
stops.quote: a very small and despised sect of Christians, known, if known at all, as Sandemanians; and our hope is founded on the faith as it is in Christ.

stops.name: Royal Institution, the letter to The Times on table-turning
stops.date_confidence: attested to 28 June 1853: the letter is a digitised primary source, Epsilon letter Faraday2691, fetched directly, and is signed 'M. Faraday, Royal Institution, June 28', which is why the stop sits at the Albemarle Street pin. The construction of the index apparatus is described in the letter itself
stops.campa: Table-turning has been in every drawing room in London for a year: hands laid flat on a table, the table moves, and the movement is credited to electricity, to magnetism, to an unknown force, to the dead. Faraday builds two boards with rollers between them and an index that shows which way the upper board is being pushed, and hands the sitters an instrument that tells them what their own muscles are doing. The tables stop turning. He writes to The Times on the twenty eighth of June and signs it from the Royal Institution.
stops.quote: I have been greatly startled by the revelation which this purely physical subject has made of the condition of the public mind.
stops.quote_source: Michael Faraday, letter to the Editor of The Times, 28 June 1853, Epsilon: The Michael Faraday Collection, letter Faraday2691

stops.name: The Thames at the City, the white cards
stops.date_confidence: [R] The letter to The Times of 7 July 1855 describing the state of the river, and the white card lowered into the water, are in the Royal Institution record; the letter itself was not fetched for this file, and details of the demonstration beyond the fact of it are tradition. The coordinates are a general City of London Thames placeholder: the exact vantage point on the river is not recorded in anything reached here
stops.campa: He takes a steamboat down the river in July and drops torn pieces of white card into the water over the side, one after another, watching how far each sinks before it goes out of sight. They disappear within an inch of the surface. The whole river is an opaque pale brown fluid moving under the bridges. He sends the observation to The Times as an observation, with no recommendation attached to it. Three years later Parliament, sitting beside the same water through a hot June, votes the money for a sewer system.

stops.name: Trinity Buoy Wharf, the workshop by the light
stops.date_confidence: [R] Wikipedia confirms that Faraday carried out experiments at Trinity Buoy Wharf and that his workshop still stands there; it does NOT confirm the pool's claim that the workshop stood above the Chain and Buoy Store. The wharf is a working yard of chain and paint and moored buoys, not an institution, and the experiments done in it are meant to end up on a rock in the sea.

stops.name: Dungeness, the first light run by a machine
stops.date_confidence: attested and UPGRADED from the pool's [R]: Dungeness was chosen by Faraday, as scientific adviser to Trinity House, to be the first lighthouse to receive a permanent electric light installation, operational 1 February 1862 and decommissioned 1 October 1875. Coordinates caveat: the pin sits near, not on, the 1961 tower, and the structure Faraday actually lit was an earlier one; the pin marks the site rather than the building
stops.campa: On the first of February the light at Dungeness is lit by electricity, a carbon arc fed from a magneto electric machine, and it is the first lighthouse anywhere in the world to hold a permanent electric light. Faraday, scientific adviser to the Corporation, has pressed for the trial and reports on how it behaves. The machine driving the arc is a direct descendant of the copper disc he set turning between the poles of a magnet in the Albemarle Street basement thirty one years before. It burns on that shingle until 1875.

stops.name: Barnsbury Grove, Islington, the last meeting house
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Sandemanian congregation relocated to Barnsbury Grove, Islington, in 1862. Month set to order the segment after Dungeness in February. The resignation of the eldership on 5 June 1864 and the end of the Trinity House role in 1865 are attested in the sources; the month of the move itself is not recorded here
stops.campa: The congregation gives up the meeting house in Paul's Alley, where it has met since 1778, and moves north to a chapel in Barnsbury Grove. Faraday goes with it. He has been its deacon and twice its elder; he resigns the eldership on the fifth of June 1864, and after that sits in the pews with no office. In 1865 he gives up Trinity House. He has already given his last Friday Discourse and his last Christmas Lecture, and the diary of experiments, numbered continuously since 1832, has stopped.

stops.name: Hampton Court Green, the last house
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 August 1867 at his home on Hampton Court Green, per the Westminster Abbey commemorations page, fetched directly. No medically certified cause is established in any source consulted for this file. The tradition that he died in his chair at the window is biographical and is [R]
stops.campa: He has been at Hampton Court in the Queen's house since 1858, doing nothing and asked to do nothing. The memory that began going at forty eight has gone entirely; he sits at a window facing the garden, knows the people who come to him, and is by every account content. Fifty two years of continuous experiment in one basement in Mayfair have stopped, and the laboratory diary, numbered straight through since 1832, ended some while ago. On the twenty fifth of August 1867 he dies in that room, seventy five years old, with Sarah beside him.

stops.name: Highgate Cemetery, the Dissenters' ground

stops.campa: The funeral is what he asked for: no procession, no address, the family only, and a plain stone. He is buried in the Dissenters' ground on the west side of Highgate Cemetery, in the plot the Sandemanian congregation keeps. The stone gives his name and the dates and nothing further. Sarah is buried with him afterwards. The story that he turned down an offer of burial in Westminster Abbey is told everywhere and documented nowhere; what is documented is that he asked for this.

stops.name: Elephant and Castle, the steel box on the roundabout
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Faraday Memorial, designed by Rodney Gordon in 1959 and constructed in 1961 at the Elephant and Castle gyratory near Faraday's birthplace, houses a London Underground electrical substation for the Northern and Bakerloo lines. This CORRECTS the research pool, which described it as a brutalist concrete monument; it is stainless steel. Month unknown, defaults to January
stops.campa: At the gyratory a short walk from where he was born, London Transport needs a substation to feed the Northern and Bakerloo lines. Rodney Gordon designs a windowless box of stainless steel to hold the transformers, and it is called the Faraday Memorial. Gordon wanted it clad in glass so that anyone crossing the road could watch the machinery working inside; the glass was dropped for fear of vandalism. So it stands in the middle of the traffic at Newington Butts, a sealed metal shell with a field inside it that nothing outside can detect.
